lead: A fragment is a reusable piece of a screen that lives inside an activity and has its own life cycle. One list-and-detail code base can fill a phone screen or half a tablet screen without being written twice. The activity owns the window; the fragment draws inside a container view the activity provides. Fragments carry most visible content of a modern Android app: lists, settings, dialogs. Their data goes in through an arguments Bundle and comes out through the host activity, and the FragmentManager adds, replaces and removes them.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.4 for the activity life cycle and Chapter 2.3 for layouts and the R class.

blocks.text: A phone is narrow, so a list and the details of one item usually need two screens. A tablet can show both at once. Writing the logic twice wastes effort and the copies drift apart.

A fragment has its own layout XML and Java class and draws inside a container view owned by an activity. The same ListFragment can fill a whole phone screen or the left half of a tablet screen. The activity stays in charge of the window; the fragment is a guest.

The activity layout holds at least one container, usually a FrameLayout such as R.id.list_container. The fragment never chooses its position; the activity's XML does. Android picks the layout by qualifier: res/layout holds the phone layout with one container, res/layout-sw600dp holds one with two containers, list_container and detail_container, used when the smallest width is at least 600 dp.

A dp (density-independent pixel) is a screen-size unit that does not change with pixel density; 1 dp is about 1/160 inch. A typical phone is about 360 dp wide, a tablet 900 dp or more. Code calls findViewById(R.id.detail_container): on the phone it returns null, on the tablet it returns the second container.

The host activity drives the fragment. Android calls these methods in this order: onAttach(Context), onCreate(Bundle), onCreateView(LayoutInflater, ViewGroup, Bundle), onViewCreated(View, Bundle), onStart(), onResume(), onPause(), onStop(), onDestroyView(), onDestroy(), onDetach().

The list splits into two halves. From onCreate to onDestroy the fragment object exists. From onCreateView to onDestroyView it has a view on screen. onCreateView must return the root View, usually by calling inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_list, container, false); onDestroyView throws that view away. A fragment parked on the back stack keeps its object and loses its view.

The callbacks are tied to the host but never equal to it. A fragment cannot resume before its activity resumes, and when the activity stops, its fragments are stopped in the same pass right after the activity's own onStop() runs. getActivity() returns the host activity, and null once onDetach has run.

Rotation destroys and recreates the activity. The FragmentManager recreates its fragments and restores their saved state, so do not keep important data in plain fields; put it in the arguments Bundle.

Every activity has a FragmentManager. Call getSupportFragmentManager() in the activity, or getParentFragmentManager() inside a fragment. The manager keeps the list of fragments attached to each container and restores them after a configuration change.
A transaction is a group of changes applied together. Begin it with beginTransaction(), which returns a FragmentTransaction.

items: add(containerId, fragment, tag): puts a new fragment into that container.
replace(containerId, fragment): removes everything in that container, then adds the new fragment.
remove(fragment): takes one fragment out of its container.
addToBackStack(name): records the transaction so Back undoes it.
commit(): sends work to the main thread and returns immediately.

blocks.text: Without addToBackStack, Back closes the whole activity instead of returning to the previous fragment. Calling commit() after onSaveInstanceState throws IllegalStateException; check isStateSaved() first, and avoid commitAllowingStateLoss() unless losing the change is safe.

Data goes in through setArguments(bundle) before the transaction, read with getArguments(); never pass data through a constructor, because the system recreates the fragment with no arguments. Data comes out through the host activity: declare an interface, let the activity implement it, call it from the fragment. Newer code uses the Fragment Result API: setFragmentResult("itemKey", bundle) on the sender and setFragmentResultListener("itemKey", this, listener) on the receiver. Never hold a direct reference to another fragment.
Three ready-made fragment types cover common screens. Each is still a fragment: same life cycle, same FragmentManager, same arguments Bundle.

items: ListFragment: its view is a ListView; call setListAdapter(adapter) and override onListItemClick. Good for short lists; newer code puts a RecyclerView inside an ordinary fragment (see Unit 3).

DialogFragment: shows a dialog window. Override onCreateDialog(Bundle) to build an AlertDialog, or onCreateView for a custom layout. It survives rotation because the FragmentManager recreates it; close it with dismiss().
PreferenceFragmentCompat: builds a settings screen from an XML preference file. It needs the AndroidX preference library and writes choices through the preference system (see Unit 4).

blocks.text: A DialogFragment can hand a result back through the Fragment Result API, which is why raw AlertDialog objects are avoided: a raw dialog is lost on rotation and the activity has no safe handle on it.

figure.caption: The 360 dp phone has one container, so tapping item 2 replaces the list with the detail and puts 1 entry on the back stack. The 900 dp tablet uses the sw600dp layout with two containers, so the detail changes beside the list and the back stack stays at 0.

examples.question: A master-detail app lists 3 items. The phone is 360 dp wide and the tablet is 900 dp wide. State which layout folder each device uses, how many fragment containers each layout has, and trace what happens when the user taps item 2 on each device. Give the back-stack size after the tap.
steps: The qualifier sw600dp matches when the device's smallest width is at least 600 dp. Phone: 360 dp < 600 dp, so res/layout/activity_main.xml is used. Tablet: 900 dp ≥ 600 dp, so res/layout-sw600dp/activity_main.xml is used.
The phone layout holds one FrameLayout, list_container; the tablet layout holds two, list_container and detail_container. Container counts are 1 and 2.
The activity adds a ListFragment of 3 items into R.id.list_container: getSupportFragmentManager().beginTransaction().add(R.id.list_container, new ListFragment()).commit().

findViewById(R.id.detail_container) returns null on the phone, so no detail fragment is added: 1 fragment on screen, back stack = 0. On the tablet it returns the second container, so the activity adds a DetailFragment with arguments item = 1. Fragments = 2, back stack = 0.

Phone tap item 2: the ListFragment calls the host's onItemSelected(2). The host builds a DetailFragment with arguments item = 2 and runs replace(R.id.list_container, detail), addToBackStack(null), commit(). The list view dies but its fragment object stays on the back stack, so back-stack size = 1.
Tablet tap item 2: the host replaces whatever sits in detail_container with a new DetailFragment with arguments item = 2, no addToBackStack. The list stays visible at left; back-stack size = 0.
examples.answer: The sw600dp threshold is 600 dp: the 360 dp phone uses 1 container and ends with 1 back-stack entry after the tap, while the 900 dp tablet uses 2 containers and ends with 0 back-stack entries.
examples.check:
SW = 600

def containers(w):
    return 2 if w >= SW else 1

def back_entries(w):
    return 0 if w >= SW else 1

print(SW)
print(containers(360))
print(containers(900))
print(back_entries(360))
print(back_entries(900))

traps: Calling getActivity() after onDetach, or getView() after onDestroyView. The fragment object may still exist on the back stack with no host and no view.
Calling commit() after onSaveInstanceState and crashing with IllegalStateException. Check isStateSaved() first.
Treating the fragment and activity life cycles as identical. A fragment on the back stack can run onDestroyView while the activity is fully resumed; the view dies, the object does not.
Passing data through a constructor. On rotation the system recreates the fragment with the no-argument constructor, so the field is empty; use setArguments and getArguments.
Calling another fragment's method directly. After rotation the saved reference points at a dead fragment object no longer attached to any window.

quiz.q: List the fragment life-cycle callbacks from onAttach to onDetach in order.
quiz.a: onAttach(Context), onCreate(Bundle), onCreateView(LayoutInflater, ViewGroup, Bundle), onViewCreated(View, Bundle), onStart(), onResume(), onPause(), onStop(), onDestroyView(), onDestroy(), onDetach().

quiz.q: What does replace(containerId, fragment) do to whatever was already in the container?
quiz.a: It removes every fragment currently in that container and adds the new one. Afterwards the container holds only the new fragment.

quiz.q: Why does a fragment have two separate halves in its life cycle?
quiz.a: One half (onCreate to onDestroy) is the fragment object; the other (onCreateView to onDestroyView) is the view it shows. A fragment on the back stack keeps its object but loses its view, so the two halves must be separable.

quiz.q: Why must data be passed into a fragment with an arguments Bundle instead of a constructor?
quiz.a: After a configuration change the FragmentManager recreates the fragment by calling its no-argument constructor. Only the arguments Bundle is saved and restored, so a constructor value would be lost.

quiz.q: A device reports a smallest width of 720 dp. Which activity layout folder does Android use for a layout that has a layout/ and a layout-sw600dp/ version, and how many containers does that layout have in a master-detail app?
quiz.a: 720 dp ≥ 600 dp, so res/layout-sw600dp/activity_main.xml is used. It has 2 containers, list_container and detail_container, so the list and the detail show side by side.

quiz.q: In the master-detail app, the phone path calls addToBackStack(null) but the tablet path does not. Why the difference?
quiz.a: On the phone the detail covers the list, so Back must undo the replace to bring the list back. On the tablet the list stays visible beside the detail, so there is nothing to undo and a back-stack entry would make Back do nothing useful.

quiz.q: A colleague stores the parsed item id in a field of the fragment and passes it to a second fragment by calling a method on a saved reference. Name two failures this causes.
quiz.a: After rotation the field is empty because the fragment is recreated without arguments, and the saved reference points to a detached fragment with no host or view. Use an arguments Bundle and the Fragment Result API instead.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production Android, most apps follow a single-activity design: one activity hosts many fragments, and the Jetpack Navigation component owns the FragmentManager transactions and the back stack. Fragments keep gaining features such as the Fragment Result API and view life-cycle-aware data collection. Jetpack Compose replaces fragments in new projects, but many existing screens still use them. Search for "single activity architecture", "Navigation component", and "Fragment lifecycle" in the official Android documentation.
